mainTopicBrief: 本单元围绕“科学家”话题，涵盖屠呦呦的坚守（Reading）、科学的自由与质疑（Extended reading：费曼演讲）和机遇与准备（Grammar：弗莱明与青霉素）三个子话题——科学家精神与创新是高考书面表达与雅思教育科技类议论文的高频命题。

subTopics.title: 坚守与突破：屠呦呦
subTopics.desc: 课文人物：the first female scientist of the PRC to receive a Nobel Prize——190次失败后 the efforts finally paid off。

prompts.task: 你校英文报开展 "The Scientist I Admire Most" 征文活动。请你写一篇短文介绍屠呦呦（Tu Youyou），内容包括：1. 她的主要成就；2. 最打动你的一点；3. 她对你的影响。注意：词数100左右。
prompts.reference:
The Scientist I Admire Most

The scientist I admire most is Tu Youyou, the first female scientist of the People's Republic of China to receive a Nobel Prize, awarded for her contribution to the fight against malaria.

What moves me most is not the prize but the road to it. It was not until the 1970s, after many failed experiments, that she succeeded in discovering qinghaosu. Facing repeated failures, she turned to ancient medical books, redesigned the experiments, and even tested the medicine on herself. Her efforts finally paid off, and malaria patients all over the world now have a greatly increased chance of survival.

From her I have learned that real success rarely comes at the first attempt — what matters is to fail, learn and try once more.
vocabHints: the first female scientist to receive
contribution to the fight against malaria
a greatly increased chance of survival

prompts.task: Some people think that government funding should only support scientific research with clear practical benefits, while others believe research without immediate applications also deserves support. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. (Write at least 250 words.)
prompts.reference:
How public money should be divided between useful science and merely curious science is a debate every research budget reopens. Some argue that taxpayers deserve visible returns — medicines, machines, measurable progress — while others insist that knowledge pursued for its own sake is the seed of every later harvest. My own view sides firmly with the second camp, though not unconditionally.

The demand for practical returns is not philistine; it is accountable. Public funds are raised from citizens with pressing needs, and a government that channels them towards malaria treatments rather than abstract puzzles can defend every pound of the choice. Applied research also disciplines science with deadlines and outcomes, and its triumphs — vaccines produced in months, crops that survive drought — are the strongest public argument science possesses.

Yet the history of discovery keeps embarrassing this logic. The research that changes the world most has repeatedly begun with no application in view: curiosity about light became the physics inside every satellite; an accidentally contaminated dish, noticed by a prepared mind, became penicillin. Practical projects spend from a bank of fundamental knowledge that someone else deposited decades earlier, and a funding policy that rewards only withdrawals will eventually empty the account. Worse, demanding declared benefits in advance teaches researchers to promise safely and think small.

My conclusion is that the two kinds of research stand in a supply chain, not a competition. Fund the practical generously — its debts fall due today. But guard a protected share for undirected curiosity, because the application no one can yet name is usually the one that matters most.

subTopics.title: 机遇与准备
subTopics.desc: 课文语篇：弗莱明发现青霉素 far from an accident——Fortune favours the prepared mind。

prompts.task: 你校英文报以 "Luck or Preparation?" 为主题征文。请你结合弗莱明发现青霉素的故事写一篇短文，内容包括：1. 简述这一发现；2. 你的观点；3. 联系自身实际。注意：词数100左右。
prompts.reference:
Luck or Preparation?

One might think Fleming discovered penicillin by accident: a dish left uncovered, a bit of mould, and — a miracle medicine! But actually this is far from the truth.

When Fleming observed that the bacteria surrounding the mould were dead, thousands had seen similar dishes and simply washed them. It was his years of research that turned an accident into a discovery. As Pasteur said, fortune favours the prepared mind.

The story speaks to me directly. I used to envy the "lucky" top students until I noticed their thick notebooks of past mistakes. Now I keep one too — because when my chance comes, I want to be the prepared mind it favours.
vocabHints: turn an accident into a discovery

prompts.task: Some people believe that success is mainly the result of luck, while others think it comes from hard work and preparation. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. (Write at least 250 words.)
prompts.reference:
Every success story invites the same quiet question: was it earned or was it lucky? One school credits fortune — the right family, the right market, the right moment; the other insists that preparation and persistence explain nearly everything. My own view is that luck deals the cards, but preparation decides who can play them.

The case for luck is stronger than winners like to admit. Birthplace, health and timing are distributed before effort begins, and identical talents meet very different doors. Two equally able students may find one school funded and the other failing; a brilliant product can sink merely by launching a season early. Honest observers concede that many who work hardest — miners, nurses, farmers — are not those rewarded most, which alone proves that effort is no guarantee.

Yet the opposing camp holds the practical truth. Luck is, by definition, beyond control, so preparation is the only variable a person can actually move. More deeply, opportunity is useless to those unready for it: the lucky accident lands on many desks, but only the prepared mind recognises what it is seeing. History's 'accidental' discoveries follow the same script — the chance event was public, the readiness was rare. Preparation, in effect, converts luck from weather into harvest; the rain falls on every field, but only the ploughed ones drink.

My conclusion is that the debate mistakes partners for rivals. Luck sets the range of what is possible; preparation determines the share of it that is claimed. The wise, accordingly, forecast less and plough more.

subTopics.title: 校园科技节
subTopics.desc: 综合技能板块核心：Science Festival goes off with a bang——从 'Planets in a bottle' 到全场 the standout activity，科学精神就在动手与惊叹之间生长。

prompts.task: 你校上周举办了首届科技节。请你用英文为校英文报写一篇报道，内容包括：1. 活动概况；2. 最受欢迎的项目；3. 同学们的收获。注意：词数100左右。
prompts.reference:
Our school's first Science Festival went off with a bang last Friday, drawing a huge crowd to the playground.

Dozens of experiments were on show, but the standout activity was "Planets in a bottle", in which students tried to create the conditions of different planets inside glass bottles. Nearby, a home-made rocket shot into the sky and won a burst of applause. Everywhere, curious faces leaned in, asked questions and tried things with their own hands.

What students gained was more than fun. As one classmate put it, science is not a list of facts to memorise, but a way of wondering about the world. Judging by the shining eyes that afternoon, our first festival will surely not be the last.
vocabHints: create the conditions of different planets
tried things with their own hands
a way of wondering about the world

prompts.task: Some people think that schools should place more emphasis on science subjects than on arts subjects such as music and painting. To what extent do you agree or disagree? (Write at least 250 words.)
prompts.reference:
Because modern economies run on technology, some argue that schools should prioritise science over arts subjects like music and painting. While I recognise the value of scientific education, I disagree that it should crowd out the arts, for a good education must develop the whole mind rather than only its useful half.

The argument for science is understandable. Scientific and mathematical skills drive innovation, create jobs and equip citizens to understand a world of data, medicine and climate. A country short of engineers and scientists will struggle economically, so ensuring strong science teaching is clearly a national priority, and few would deny it a central place in the timetable.

However, treating the arts as dispensable is a serious mistake. Music, painting and drama develop creativity, emotional intelligence and cultural understanding — qualities that science itself increasingly depends upon, since breakthroughs demand imagination as much as calculation. The arts also give life meaning beyond productivity; a society of skilled technicians who cannot appreciate beauty or express feeling would be prosperous but impoverished. For many students, moreover, the arts are where confidence and identity are first discovered.

The wiser aim is balance, not dominance. Science and the arts train different but complementary capacities, and the most creative scientists and thoughtful citizens are usually those exposed to both.

In conclusion, while science deserves strong support because of its practical importance, it should not be promoted at the expense of the arts. An education that feeds only the analytical mind and starves the imagination prepares students for a job, but not fully for a life.

subTopics.title: 质疑的自由
subTopics.desc: 课文演讲：费曼 Permit us to question — to doubt — to not be sure——科学的价值在于自由思想。

prompts.task: 你校科技节将举办以 "Dare to Doubt" 为主题的英语演讲比赛。请你撰写演讲稿，内容包括：1. 你对“质疑精神”的理解；2. 一个事例（科学史或身边事）；3. 向同学发出号召。注意：词数100左右。
prompts.reference:
Dare to Doubt

Good afternoon, everyone!

What makes science move forward? Not the answers we memorize, but the questions we dare to ask. As a great physicist said, we scientists take it for granted that it is perfectly possible to live and not know — doubt is not to be feared, but to be welcomed and discussed.

Let me share a small story. Last term, I found my textbook's data on local rainfall outdated. Instead of copying it, I emailed the weather bureau, got the latest figures, and my report earned the top mark — plus a thank-you letter from the publisher!

So, my friends, permit yourselves to question, to doubt, to not be sure. That is where every discovery begins. Thank you!
vocabHints: doubt is not to be feared but to be welcomed

prompts.task: Some people believe that students should accept what their teachers tell them, while others think students should question everything they are taught. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. (Write at least 250 words.)
prompts.reference:
Whether the classroom should train acceptance or doubt is an old tension in education, sharpened now by a world where information multiplies faster than any teacher can filter it. Some hold that students learn best by trusting instruction; others urge them to question everything. My view is that both slogans fail as absolutes, and the real skill lies in knowing when each is due.

The case for acceptance rests on the economics of learning. Knowledge is cumulative: a student who re-litigates every fact will never reach the frontier where questioning becomes productive. Trust is also the classroom's working currency — teachers compress centuries of tested knowledge into usable form, and treating every lesson as suspect wastes that inheritance while exhausting both sides. No one relearns arithmetic by scepticism.

Yet a schooling of pure acceptance produces exactly the citizens the modern world cannot afford: fluent recallers who cannot tell evidence from authority. Questioning is not disrespect; it is the method by which knowledge was built in the first place, and every scientific revolution began with someone doubting what every teacher then taught. More practically, students who ask 'how do we know this?' retain understanding rather than answers — and understanding is what survives after examinations end.

My conclusion is that the object of education is neither obedience nor rebellion but calibrated doubt: accept provisionally, question methodically. Teachers serve this best not by demanding belief but by showing their working, inviting challenge and rewarding the student who finds the weak joint. The best classroom does not fear the raised hand; it is built around it.
